column1: # Hyperion syscall inventory — canonical classification data
# One row per canonical syscall. This is the single source of truth from which
# docs/syscalls/U1..U4.md and E1..E3.md are generated by tools/gen_syscall_inventory.py.
# Do not edit the generated Markdown by hand; edit this file and regenerate.
# Columns (tab-separated):
#   nr      x86-64 syscall number (common/64 ABI). Must exist in
#           docs/syscalls/kernel-table-x86_64-6.12.tsv with abi common|64.
#   name    syscall name (matches the kernel table).
#   tier    U4 | U3 | U2 | U1 | E1 | E2 | E3
#   status  not-started | stubbed | implemented | validated
#   purpose one-line description of what the call does.
#   evidence  how the tier was assigned: "trace:N" (observed N times in the
#           Phase 6 strace sweep), or "provisional" (no direct measurement yet).
# Tier criteria (see docs/syscalls/README.md for the full text):
#   Usage tiers rank how likely an ordinary userspace program is to call the
#   syscall, from highest to lowest frequency:
#     U4 called by nearly every process or on a hot path
#     U3 called by most substantial programs
#     U2 called by many programs, or only on particular operations
#     U1 called rarely: legacy-but-live, or narrow tooling only
#   Extra categories classify by role, NOT frequency:
#     E1 high-value additions essential to x86-64 process/ABI compatibility or
#        to specific important workloads, which do not fit a frequency band
#     E2 specialized/optional subsystems (SysV IPC, POSIX mq, AIO, NUMA,
#        keyrings, extended attributes, modern eventfd/timerfd/signalfd, io_uring)
#     E3 rare, legacy, obsolete, privileged or reserved calls that normal
#        userspace must never need
# nr
